entries.b3f6592e4a4a78078d51ffb910a0289f1c9944b8: <div sID="gen5894" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="29" osisID="1Sam.29" sID="1Sam.29"/> <div eID="gen5894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5895" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5896" type="x-p"/> How Saul, who was forsaken of God, when he was in a strait was more and more perplexed and embarrassed with his own counsels, we read in the foregoing chapter. In this chapter we find how David, who kept close to God, when he was in a strait was extricated and brought off by the providence of God, without any contrivance of his own. We have him, I. Marching with the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1-1Sam.29.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. Excepted against by the lords of the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.3-1Sam.29.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. III. Happily dismissed by Achish from that service which did so ill become him, and which yet he knew not how to decline, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.6-1Sam.29.11">ver. 6-11</reference>.
entries.86d3abd90035b274323f5cd87ed121e021bfab15: <div eID="gen5896" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5895" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David with the Philistines. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen5897" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now the Philistines gathered together all their armies to Aphek: and the Israelites pitched by a fountain which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Jezreel. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the lords of the Philistines passed on by hundreds, and by thousands: but David and his men passed on in the rereward with Achish. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then said the princes of the Philistines, What <hi type="italic">do</hi> these Hebrews <hi type="italic">here?</hi> And Achish said unto the princes of the Philistines, <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not this David, the servant of Saul the king of Israel, which hath been with me these days, or these years, and I have found no fault in him since he fell <hi type="italic">unto me</hi> unto this day? <hi type="super">4</hi> And the princes of the Philistines were wroth with him; and the princes of the Philistines said unto him, Make this fellow return, that he may go again to his place which thou hast appointed him, and let him not go down with us to battle, lest in the battle he be an adversary to us: for wherewith should he reconcile himself unto his master? <hi type="italic">should it</hi> not <hi type="italic">be</hi> with the heads of these men? <hi type="super">5</hi> <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not this David, of whom they sang one to another in dances, saying, Saul slew his thousands, and David his ten thousands? <div eID="gen5897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5898" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The great strait that David was in, which we may suppose he himself was aware of, though we read not of his asking advice from God, nor of any project of his own to get clear of it. The two armies of the Philistines and the Israelites were encamped and ready to engage, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1">v. 1</reference>. Achish, who had been kind to David, had obliged him to come himself and bring the forces he had into his service. David came accordingly, and, upon a review of the army, was found with Achish, in the post assigned him in the rear, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.2">v. 2</reference>. Now, 1. If, when the armies engaged, he should retire, and quit his post, he would fall under the indelible reproach, not only of cowardice and treachery, but of base ingratitude to Achish, who had been his protector and benefactor and had reposed a confidence in him, and from whom he had received a very honourable commission. Such an unprincipled thing as this he could by no means persuade himself to do. 2. If he should, as was expected from him, fight for the Philistines against Israel, he would incur the imputation of being an enemy to the Israel of God and a traitor to his country, would make his own people hate him, and unanimously oppose his coming to the crown, as unworthy the name of an Israelite, much more the honour and trust of a king of Israel, when he had fought against them under the banner of the uncircumcised. If Saul should be killed (as it proved he was) in this engagement, the fault would be laid at David's door, as if he had killed him. So that on each side there seemed to be both sin and scandal. This was the strait he was in; and a great strait it was to a good man, greater to see sin before him than to see trouble. Into this strait he brought himself by his own unadvisedness, in quitting the land of Judah, and going among the uncircumcised. It is strange if those that associate themselves with wicked people, and grow intimate with them, come off without guilt, or grief, or both. What he himself proposed to do does not appear. Perhaps he designed to act only as keeper to the king's head, the post assigned him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.2">ch. xxviii. 2</reference>) and not to do any thing offensively against Israel. But it would have been very hard to come so near the brink of sin and not to fall in. Therefore, though God might justly have left him in this difficulty, to chastise him for his folly, yet, because his heart was upright with him, he would <hi type="italic">not suffer him to be tempted above what he was able, but with the temptation made a way for him to escape,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">1 Cor. x. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen5898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5899" type="x-p"/> II. A door opened for his deliverance out of this strait. God inclined the hearts of the princes of the Philistines to oppose his being employed in the battle, and to insist upon his being dismissed. Thus their enmity befriended him, when no friend he had was capable of doing him such a kindness. 1. It was a proper question which they asked, upon the mustering of the forces, "<hi type="italic">What do these Hebrews here?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.3">v. 3</reference>. What confidence can we put in them, or what service can we expect from them?" A <hi type="italic">Hebrew is out of his place,</hi> and, if he has the spirit of a <hi type="italic">Hebrew, is out of his element,</hi> when he is in the camp of the Philistines, and deserves to be made uneasy there. David used to <hi type="italic">hate the congregation of evil doers,</hi> however he came now to be among them, <reference osisRef="Ps.26.5">Ps. xxvi. 5</reference>. It was an honourable testimony which Achish, on this occasion, gave to David. He looked upon him as a refugee, that fled from a wrongful prosecution in his own country, and had put himself under his protection, whom therefore he was obliged, in justice, to take care of, and thought he might in prudence employ; "for (says he) he has been with me <hi type="italic">these days,</hi> or <hi type="italic">these years,</hi>" that is, a considerable time, many days at his court and a year or two in his country, and he never found any fault in him, nor saw any cause to distrust his fidelity, or to think any other than that he had heartily come over to him. By this it appears that David had conducted himself with a great deal of caution, and had prudently concealed the affection he still retained for his own people. We have need to <hi type="italic">walk in wisdom towards those that are without, to keep our mouth when the wicked is before us,</hi> and to be upon the reserve. 3. Yet the princes are peremptory in it, that he must be sent home; and they give good reasons for their insisting on it. (1.) Because he had been an old enemy to the Philistines; witness what was sung in honour of his triumphs over them: <hi type="italic">Saul slew his thousands, and David his ten thousands,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.5">v. 5</reference>. "It will be a reproach to us to harbour and trust so noted a destroyer of our people; nor can it be thought that he will now act heartily against Saul who then acted so vigorously with him and for him." Who would be fond of popular praise or applause when, even that may, another time, be turned against a man to his reproach? (2.) Because he might be a most dangerous enemy to them, and do them more mischief then all Saul's army could (<reference osisRef="1Sam.29.4">v. 4</reference>): "He may <hi type="italic">in the battle be an adversary to us,</hi> and surprise us with an attack in the rear, while their army charges us in the front; and we have reason to think he will do so, that, by betraying us, he may reconcile himself to his master. Who can trust a man who, besides his affection to his country, will think it his interest to be false to us?" It is dangerous to put confidence in a reconciled enemy.
entries.028e0cee74b9bf2b3c47c42b4868bf7365367911: <div eID="gen5899" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Leaves the Philistines. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen5900" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Then Achish called David, and said unto him, Surely, <hi type="italic">as</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, thou hast been upright, and thy going out and thy coming in with me in the host <hi type="italic">is</hi> good in my sight: for I have not found evil in thee since the day of thy coming unto me unto this day: nevertheless the lords favour thee not. <hi type="super">7</hi> Wherefore now return, and go in peace, that thou displease not the lords of the Philistines. <hi type="super">8</hi> And David said unto Achish, But what have I done? and what hast thou found in thy servant so long as I have been with thee unto this day, that I may not go fight against the enemies of my lord the king? <hi type="super">9</hi> And Achish answered and said to David, I know that thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> good in my sight, as an angel of God: notwithstanding the princes of the Philistines have said, He shall not go up with us to the battle. <hi type="super">10</hi> Wherefore now rise up early in the morning with thy master's servants that are come with thee: and as soon as ye be up early in the morning, and have light, depart. <hi type="super">11</hi> So David and his men rose up early to depart in the morning, to return into the land of the Philistines. And the Philistines went up to Jezreel. <div eID="gen5900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5901" type="x-p"/> If the reasons Achish had to trust David were stronger than the reasons which the princes offered why they should distrust him (as I do not see that, in policy, they were, for the princes were certainly in the right), yet Achish was but one of five, though the chief, and the only one that had the title of king; accordingly, in a council of war held on this occasion, he was over-voted, and obliged to dismiss David, though he was extremely fond of him. Kings cannot always do as they would, nor have such as they would about them. <div eID="gen5901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5902" type="x-p"/> I. The discharge Achish gives him is very honourable, and not a final discharge, but only from the present service. 1. He signifies the great pleasure and satisfaction he had taken in him and in his conversation: <hi type="italic">Thou art good in my sight as an angel of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.9">v. 9</reference>. Wise and good men will gain respect, wherever they go, from all that know how to make a right estimate of persons and things, though of different professions in religion. What Achish says of David, God, by the prophet, says <hi type="italic">of the house of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.8">Zech. xii. 8</reference>), that it shall be <hi type="italic">as the angel of the Lord.</hi> But the former is a court-compliment; the latter is a divine promise. 2. He gives him a testimonial of his good behaviour, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.6">v. 6</reference>. It is very full and in obliging terms: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast been upright,</hi> and thy whole conduct has been <hi type="italic">good in my sight,</hi> and <hi type="italic">I have not found evil in thee.</hi>" Saul would not have given him such a testimonial, though he had done far more service to him than Achish. God's people should behave themselves always so inoffensively as if possible to get the good word of all they have dealings with; and it is a debt we owe to those who have acquitted themselves well to give them the praise of it. 3. He lays all the blame of his dismission upon the princes, who would by no means suffer him to continue in the camp. "The king loves thee entirely, and would venture his life in thy hand; <hi type="italic">but the lords favour thee not,</hi> and we must not disoblige them, nor can we oppose them; therefore <hi type="italic">return and go in peace.</hi>" He had better part with his favourite than occasion a disgust among his generals and a mutiny in his army. Achish intimates a reason why they were uneasy. It was not so much for David's own sake as for the sake of his soldiers that attended him, whom he calls <hi type="italic">his master's servants</hi> (namely, Saul's), <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.10">v. 10</reference>. They could trust him, but not them. (4.) He orders him to be gone early, as soon as it was light (<reference osisRef="1Sam.29.10">v. 10</reference>), to prevent their further resentments, and the jealousies they would have been apt to conceive if he had lingered. <div eID="gen5902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5903" type="x-p"/> II. His reception of this discourse is very complimental; but, I fear, not without some degree of dissimulation. "What?" says David, "must I leave <hi type="italic">my lord the king,</hi> whom I am bound by office to protect, just now when he is going to expose himself in the field? Why may not I go and <hi type="italic">fight against the enemies of my lord the king?</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.8">v. 8</reference>. He seemed anxious to serve him when he was at this juncture really anxious to leave him, but he was not willing that Achish should know that he was. No one knows how strong the temptation is to compliment and dissemble which those are in that attend great men, and how hard it is to avoid it. <div eID="gen5903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5904" type="x-p"/> III. God's providence ordered it wisely and graciously for him. For, besides that the snare was broken and he was delivered out of the dilemma to which he was first reduced, it proved a happy hastening of him to the relief of his own city, which sorely wanted him, though he did not know it. Thus the disgrace which the lords of the Philistines put upon him prove, in more ways than one, an advantage to him. <hi type="italic">The steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord, and he delighteth in his way.</hi> What he does with us we know not now, but we shall know hereafter, and shall see it was all for good.  <chapter eID="1Sam.29"/> <div eID="gen5904" type="x-p"/>

entries.280d4f98d44b78156b9db1cdda80ee7f2c596978: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2801"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 29</title> <div sID="gen3842" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1-1Sam.29.5">1Sa 29:1-5</reference>. David Marching with the Philistines to Fight with Israel.<div eID="gen3842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3843" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2801"/><hi type="bold">1. Aphek--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Josh.12.8">Jos 12:8</reference>), in the tribe of Issachar, and in the plain of Esdraelon. A person who compares the Bible account of Saul's last battle with the Philistines, with the region around Gilboa, has the same sort of evidence that the account relates what is true, that a person would have that such a battle as Waterloo really took place. Gilboa, Jezreel, Shunem, En-dor, are all found, still bearing the same names. They lie within sight of each other. Aphek is the only one of the cluster not yet identified. Jezreel on the northern slope of Gilboa, and at the distance of twenty minutes to the east, is a large fountain, and a smaller one still nearer; just the position which a chieftain would select, both on account of its elevation and the supply of water needed for his troops [Hackett, Scripture Illustrated]. <div eID="gen3843" type="x-p"/>
entries.70814e40f60783711982063273f4207c499a4a9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2802"/><div sID="gen3844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2802"/><hi type="bold">2. David and his men passed on in the rereward with Achish--</hi>as the commander of the lifeguards of Achish, who was general of this invading army of the Philistines. <div eID="gen3844" type="x-p"/>
entries.afd1a5f79199181ca43210496a44c727d4db8ecd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2803"/><div sID="gen3845" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2803"/><hi type="bold">3. these days, or these years--</hi>He had now been with the Philistines a full year and four months (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.7">1Sa 27:7</reference>), and also some years before. It has been thought that David kept up a private correspondence with this Philistine prince, either on account of his native generosity, or in the anticipation that an asylum in his territories would sooner or later be needed. <div eID="gen3845" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a4607723581090a2be26cdb60c26c83707dfb20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2804"/><div sID="gen3846" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2804"/><hi type="bold">4. the princes of the Philistines were wroth with him--</hi>It must be considered a happy circumstance in the overruling providence of God to rescue David out of the dangerous dilemma in which he was now placed. But David is not free from censure in his professions to Achish (<reference osisRef="1Sam.29.8">1Sa 29:8</reference>), to do what he probably had not the smallest purpose of doing--of fighting with Achish against his enemies. It is just an instance of the unhappy consequences into which a false step--a departure from the straight course of duty--will betray everyone who commits it. <div eID="gen3846" type="x-p"/>
entries.379565927327a727e873f582a39721a5349f5c15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2805"/><div sID="gen3847" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2805"/><hi type="bold">9. notwithstanding the princes of the Philistines have said--</hi>The Philistine government had constitutional checks--or at least the king was not an absolute sovereign; but his authority was limited--his proceedings liable to be controlled by "the powerful barons of that rude and early period--much as the kings of Europe in the Middle Ages were by the proud and lawless aristocracy which surrounded them" [Chalmers]. <chapter eID="1Sam.29"/>

entries.33ce602e5868105e053475c211185bb4c3d5630b: <div eID="gen10553" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10554" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10555" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10555" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10554" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10556" type="x-p"/> The Philistines gather their armies together against Israel, and encamp at Aphek; while the Israelites encamp at Jezreel, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1">1Sam 29:1</reference>. The lords of the Philistines refuse to let David go to battle with them, lest he should betray them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.2-1Sam.29.5">1Sam 29:2-5</reference>. Achish expresses his confidence in David; but begs him to return, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.6-1Sam.29.10">1Sam 29:6-10</reference>. David and his men return, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.11">1Sam 29:11</reference>. <div eID="gen10556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10557" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10558" type="x-p"/> To Aphek - This was a place in the valley of Jezreel, between Mounts Tabor and Gilboa. <div eID="gen10558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10559" type="x-p"/> Pitched by a fountain - To be near a fountain, or copious spring of water, was a point of great importance to an army in countries such as these, where water was so very scarce. It is supposed, as William of Tyre says, that it was at this same fountain that Saladin pitched his camp, while Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, pitched his by another fountain between Nazareth and Sephoris; each being anxious to secure that without which it was impossible for their armies to subsist.
entries.92cdca4f613f8451a9ce991e05b351b6b5c58bc9: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10560" type="x-p"/> By hundreds, and by thousands - They were probably divided, as the Jewish armies, by fifties, hundreds, and thousands; each having its proper officer or captain.
entries.a1f2e3b59d600e8d344ffc302212218e1767fb35: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10561" type="x-p"/> These days, or these years - I suppose these words to mark no definite time, and may be understood thus: "Is not this David, who has been with me for a considerable time?"
entries.3fa36d57068d0eff443fd90256ed86b02f6d3da4: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10562" type="x-p"/> The princes of the Philistines were wroth - It is strange that they had not yet heard of David's destruction of a village of the Geshurites, Gezrites, and Amalekites, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.8">1Sam 27:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.9">1Sam 27:9</reference>. Had they heard of this, they would have seen much more cause for suspicion.
entries.2a8c4de9a2fa606c03a8cb3a555800e7449553b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10563" type="x-p"/> Thou hast been upright - So he thought, for as yet he had not heard of the above transaction; David having given him to understand that he had been fighting against Israel.
entries.bc7b87388db7c15344261d77d228824a3e62af2f: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen10563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10564" type="x-p"/> David said - what have I done? - Dr. Chandler and others may say what they will to make David act a consistent part in this business; but it is most evident, whatever his intentions might be as to the part he was to take in the approaching battle, he did intend to persuade Achish that he would fight against Israel; and affects to feel his reputation injured by not being permitted on this occasion to show his fidelity to the king of Gath. <div eID="gen10564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10565" type="x-p"/> It was in the order of God's gracious providence that the Philistine lords refused to let David go with them to this battle. Had he gone, he had his choice of two sins - First, If he had fought for the Philistines, he would have fought against God and his country. Secondly If he had in the battle gone over to the Israelites, he would have deceived and become a traitor to the hospitable Achish. God, therefore, so ordered it in his mercy that he was not permitted to go to a battle in which he was sure to be disgraced, whatever side he took, or with what success soever he might be crowned.
entries.8a0a5de93bb5dcfdb39a20fcf8cc5505fd049d51: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen10565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10566" type="x-p"/> As an angel of God - There is some reason to think that Achish had actually embraced or was favourably disposed towards the Jewish religion. He speaks here of the angels of God, as a Jew might be expected to speak; and in <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.6">1Sam 29:6</reference> he appeals to, and swears by Jehovah; which, perhaps, no Philistine ever did. It is possible that he might have learned many important truths from David, during the time he sojourned with him.
entries.36e89913a986f9a19637f245a463df95326baf3b: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10567" type="x-p"/> With thy master's servants - Who were these? has been very properly asked; and to this question there can be but two answers: - <div eID="gen10567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10568" type="x-p"/> 1. The six hundred Israelites which were with him; and who might still be considered the subjects of Saul, though now residing in a foreign land. <div eID="gen10568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10569" type="x-p"/> 2. The servants of achish; i.e., David's men thus considered; because on his coming to Gath, he had in effect given up himself and his men to Achish. But Saul may be the master to whom Achish refers, and the words convey a delicate information to David that he is no vassal, but still at liberty.  <chapter eID="1Sam.29"/> <div eID="gen10569" type="x-p"/>

entries.12c1a4e6868b877df33640b1ef7e426631dca124: <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1">1Sa 29:1</reference> <div eID="gen4171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4172" type="x-p"/> The account of this is introduced by a fuller description of the position of the hostile army. “<hi type="italic">The Philistines gathered all their armies together towards Aphek, but Israel encamped at the fountain in</hi> (at) <hi type="italic">Jezreel</hi>.” This fountain is the present <hi type="italic">Ain Jalûd</hi> (or <hi type="italic">Ain Jalût</hi>, i.e., Goliath’s fountain, probably so called because it was regarded as the scene of the defeat of Goliath), a very large fountain, which issues from a cleft in the rock at the foot of the mountain on the north-eastern border of Gilboa, forming a beautifully limpid pool of about forty or fifty feet in diameter, and then flowing in a brook through the valley (Rob. <hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. iii. p. 168). Consequently <hi type="italic">Aphek</hi>, which must be carefully distinguished from the towns of the same name in Asher (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.30">Jos 19:30</reference>; Jdg 1:31) and upon the mountains of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.53">Jos 15:53</reference>) and also at Ebenezer (<reference osisRef="1Sam.4.1">1Sa 4:1</reference>), is to be sought for not very far from <hi type="italic">Shunem</hi>, in the plain of Jezreel; according to Van de Velde’s <hi type="italic">Mem</hi>., by the side of the present <hi type="italic">el Afûleh</hi>, though the situation has not been exactly determined. The statement in the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>., “near Endor of Jezreel where Saul fought,” is merely founded upon the Septuagint, in which בּעין is erroneously rendered ἐν Ἐνδώρ.
entries.22d22119a027d5943228e4df1c2972914ff0e5d6: <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.2-1Sam.29.3">1Sa 29:2-3</reference> <div eID="gen4172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4173" type="x-p"/> When the princes of the Philistines (<hi type="italic">sarne</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.3">Jos 13:3</reference>) advanced by hundreds and thousands (i.e., arranged in companies of hundreds and thousands), and David and his men came behind with Achish (i.e., forming the rear-guard), the (other) princes pronounced against their allowing David and his men to go with them. The did not occur at the time of their setting out, but on the road, when they had already gone some distance (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.11">1Sa 29:11</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.1">1Sa 30:1</reference>), probably when the five princes (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.3">Jos 13:3</reference>) of the Philistines had effected a junction. To the inquiry, “<hi type="italic">What are these Hebrews doing?</hi>” Achish replied, “<hi type="italic">Is not this David, the servant of Saul the king of Israel, who has been with me days already, or years already? and I have found nothing in him since his coming over unto this day</hi>.” מאוּמה, anything at all that could render his suspicious, or his fidelity doubtful. נפל, to fall away and go over to a person; generally construed with אל (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.13">Jer 37:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.19">Jer 38:19</reference>, etc.) or על (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">Jer 21:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.14">Jer 37:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.19-1Chr.12.20">1Ch 12:19-20</reference>), but here absolutely, as the more precise meaning can be gathered from the context.
entries.741662eac95bd268dd5c802316e4797a7f0d687b: <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.4">1Sa 29:4</reference> <div eID="gen4173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4174" type="x-p"/> But the princes, i.e., the four other princes of the Philistines, not the courtiers of Achish himself, were angry with Achish, and demanded, “<hi type="italic">Send the man back, that he may return to his place, which thou hast assigned him; that he may not go down with us into the war, and may not become an adversary</hi> (<hi type="italic">satan</hi>) <hi type="italic">to us in the war; for wherewith could he show himself acceptable to his lord</hi> (viz., Saul), <hi type="italic">if not with the heads of these men?</hi>” הלוא, <hi type="italic">nonne</hi>, strictly speaking, introduces a new question to confirm the previous question. “<hi type="italic">Go down to the battle</hi>:” this expression is used as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.10">1Sa 26:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.24">1Sa 30:24</reference>, because battles were generally fought in the plains, into which the Hebrews were obliged to come down from their mountainous land. “<hi type="italic">These men</hi>,” i.e., the soldiers of the Philistines, to whom the princes were pointing.
entries.4f0e66b1789ae23894fb1a1b7431ff7048142838: <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.5">1Sa 29:5</reference> <div eID="gen4174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4175" type="x-p"/> To justify their suspicion, the princes reminded him of their song with which the women in Israel had celebrated David’s victory over Goliath (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.7">1Sa 18:7</reference>). <div eID="gen4175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4176" type="x-p"/> After this declaration on the part of the princes, Achish was obliged to send David back.
entries.8e9b7ca4530131bc0eb0cc105d8cfa90400922f2: <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.6-1Sam.29.7">1Sa 29:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen4176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4177" type="x-p"/> With a solemn assertion, - swearing by Jehovah to convince David all the more thoroughly of the sincerity of his declaration, - Achish said to him, “<hi type="italic">Thou art honourable, and good in my eyes</hi> (i.e., quite right in my estimation) <hi type="italic">are thy going out and coming in</hi> (i.e., all thy conduct) <hi type="italic">with me in the camp, for I have not found anything bad in thee; but in the eyes of the princes thou art not good</hi> (i.e., the princes do not think thee honourable, do not trust thee). <hi type="italic">Turn now, and go in peace, that thou mayest do nothing displeasing to the princes of the Philistines</hi>.”
entries.50dd0482c9d4d6ea013f9239f36af460a155c57d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.8-1Sam.29.9">1Sa 29:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen4177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4178" type="x-p"/> Partly for the sake of vindicating himself against this suspicion, and partly to put the sincerity of Achish’s words to the test, David replied, “<hi type="italic">What have I done, and what hast thou found in thy servant, since I was with thee till this day, that I am not to come and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?</hi>” These last words are also ambiguous, since the king whom David calls his lord might be understood as meaning either Achish or Saul. Achish, in his goodness of heart, applies them without suspicion to himself; for he assures David still more earnestly (<reference osisRef="1Sam.29.9">1Sa 29:9</reference>), that he is firmly convinced of his uprightness. “<hi type="italic">I know that thou art good in my eyes as an angel of God</hi>,” i.e., I have the strongest conviction that thou hast behaved as well towards me as an angel could; but the princes have desired thy removal.
entries.d8399f5281e11069292595a4dee7c6970a856841: <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.10">1Sa 29:10</reference> <div eID="gen4178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4179" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And now get up early in the morning with the servants of thy lord</hi> (i.e., Saul, whose subjects David’s men all were), <hi type="italic">who have come with thee; get ye up in the morning when it gets light for you</hi> (so that ye can see), <hi type="italic">and go</hi>.”
entries.8f3c467a77c11963ebd86bfb865fac277ab3acd5: <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.11">1Sa 29:11</reference> <div eID="gen4179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4180" type="x-p"/> In accordance with this admonition, David returned the next morning into the land of the Philistines, i.e., to Ziklag; no doubt very light of heart, and praising God for having so graciously rescued him out of the disastrous situation into which he had been brought and not altogether without some fault of his own, rejoicing that “he had not committed either sin, i.e., had neither violated the fidelity which he owed to Achish, nor had to fight against the Israelites” (Seb. Schmidt).  <chapter eID="1Sam.29"/> <div eID="gen4180" type="x-p"/>

entries.b1767be8d6f6aa860926c34b99b552ce8e94b9b5:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="29" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XXIX.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>NOW the Philistines gathered together all their armies to Aphek <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Either, that in the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Asher, Ios.</ns0:hi> 19. 24. or ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther another Town of that Name in <ns0:hi>Issachar,</ns0:hi> though not mentioned elsewhere in Scripture; this being the case of many places, to be but once Named.</ns0:note>: and the Israelites pitch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by a fountain which <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in Jezreel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And the lords of the Philistines passed on by hundreds, and by thousands: but David, and his men passed on the rereward with Achish <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> As the Life-guard of <ns0:hi>Achish,</ns0:hi> as he had promised, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 28. 2. <ns0:hi>Achish</ns0:hi> being, as it seems, th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> General of the Army.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Then said the princes of the Philistines <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Lords of the other eminent Cities and Territories, who were confederate with him in this expedition.</ns0:note>, What <ns0:hi>do</ns0:hi> these Hebrews <ns0:hi>here?</ns0:hi> And Achish said un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to the princes of the Philistines, <ns0:hi>Is</ns0:hi> not this David the servant of Saul the king of Israel, which hath been with me these days, or these years <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Q. d.</ns0:hi> did I say <ns0:hi>Days?</ns0:hi> I might have said <ns0:hi>Years;</ns0:hi> either because he hath now been with me <ns0:hi>a full Year and four Months, chap.</ns0:hi> 27. 7. or because he was with me some Years ago, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 21. 10. and since that time hath been known to me. And it is not improbable, but <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> after his escape from thence, might hold some correspondency with <ns0:hi>Achish,</ns0:hi> as finding him to be a Man of more generous temper than the rest of the <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> and supposing that he might have need of him for a Refuge in case <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> continued to seek his life.</ns0:note>, and I have <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> nothing in him, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 14. 30.</ns0:note> found no fault in him, since he fell <ns0:hi>unto me</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Since he revolted, or left his own King to turn to me. For that sense <ns0:hi>Achish</ns0:hi> put upon this escape of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> (as it is cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 27. 1.) and so is the Phrase of <ns0:hi>falling to</ns0:hi> a party, elsewhere used, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 37. 13, 14.</ns0:note>, unto this day.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And the princes of the Philistines were wroth with him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Were unsatisfied and offended with <ns0:hi>Achish</ns0:hi> for this in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tention and declaration.</ns0:note>, and the princes of the Philistines said unto him, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chr. 12. 19.</ns0:note> Make this fellow return, that he may go again to his place which thou hast appointed him <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Herein the Wi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e and Gracious Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vidence of God appeared, both in helping him out of those snares and difficulties, out of which no human wit could have extricated him, but he must either have been, or have been thought to be a Traitor, and an ungrateful unworthy person either to the one or to the other side; and moreover in giving him the happy opportunity of recovering his own, and his All from the <ns0:hi>Amalekites,</ns0:hi> which had been irrecover<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ably lost, if he had gone into this Battel. And the kindness of God to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was the greater, because it had been <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ust for God to have left<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> in all those Distresses into which his own sinful counsel and course had brought him.</ns0:note>, and let him not go down with us to bat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tel, lest in the battel he be an adversary to us: for wherewith should he reconcile himself unto his master? <ns0:hi>should</ns0:hi> it not <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> with the heads of these men <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Of these our Soldiers? They speak according to the rules of Reason and true Policy; for by this very course, great Enemies have sometimes been reconciled together.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:hi>Is</ns0:hi> not this David, of whom they sang one to another in dances, saying, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 18. 7. and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>1. 11.</ns0:note> Saul slew his thou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sands, and David his ten thousands?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 ¶ Then Achish called David, and said unto him, Surely, <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> the LORD liveth <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">He Swears by <ns0:hi>Iehovah;</ns0:hi> either, because he did acknow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge their <ns0:hi>Iehovah</ns0:hi> to be a God, being, it may be, convinced and instructed therein by <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> though he did worship <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gon</ns0:hi> with him, and above him: or, because this was <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s God, and therefore he Swore by him; partly, out of com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plaisance with <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> that he might receive his unwelcome message to him with less offence; and partly, that this Oath might gain more credit to his words with <ns0:hi>David.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, thou hast been upright, and thy going out, and thy coming in with me <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Thy whole conversation with me. See <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 18. 13. and ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny other place where that Phrase is used.</ns0:note> in the host <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> good in my <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ight: for I have not found evil in thee, since the day of thy coming unto me <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Though before that time there was Evil in thee towards me and my people.</ns0:note>, unto this day: nevertheless <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> thou art not good in the eyes of the lords.</ns0:note> the lords favour thee not.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Wherefore now return and go in peace, that thou <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> do <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>vil in the e<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>es of the lords.</ns0:note> displease not the lords of the Philistines.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 ¶ And David said unto Achish, But what have I done? and what hast thou found in thy servant so long as I have been <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> before thee.</ns0:note> with thee unto this day, that I may not go to fight against the enemies of my lord the king <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This was deep dissimulation and flattery, but he ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prehended it necessary, lest he should tacitly confess himself guilty of that whereof they accused him, and thereby ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pose himself to the utmost hazards. These perplexities he brought himself into by his irregular course, in forsaking the Land of <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> where God had placed him, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 22. 5. and promised him protection, and putting himself into the hands of the <ns0:hi>Philistines.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And Achish answered, and said to David, I know thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> good in my sight, as an angel of God <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">In whom nothing is blame-worthy. Or, it may be used to express <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s great wisdom; (as well as integrity) as 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 14. 17. and 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 27. The <ns0:hi>Heathens</ns0:hi> acknow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledged good Spirits, which also they worshiped as an infe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rior sort of Deities, who were Messengers and Ministers to the Supreme God; onely <ns0:hi>Achish</ns0:hi> had learned the title of Angels, from the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> his Neighbours, and especially from <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s conversation.</ns0:note>: notwithstanding the princes of the Phili<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stines have said, He shall not go up with us to the battel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Wherefore now rise up early in the morning, with thy masters servants <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">He intimates the ground of the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> jealousie con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and his men, that they were all Servants of <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> and therefore had an Obligation, and were suspected to have an Affection to their old Lord and Master, against whom even <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> himself could not make them Fight, espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially with, and for the <ns0:hi>Philistines.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> that are come with thee: and assoon as ye be up early in the morning, and have light, depart <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Before the Battel be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gin, lest, if you delay, the Lords of the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> fall upon you, and destroy you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 So David and his men rose up early to depart in the morning, to return into the land of the Philistines, and the Philistines went up to Jez<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />reel.</ns0:p>
